historical_timeline.summary: Elected to the U.S. House of Representatives.
Keynote address at the Democratic National Convention.
Walking with a cane in her last House years, attributed at the time to a knee problem.
Left the House; became a professor at the LBJ School of Public Affairs; multiple sclerosis diagnosed around this time, as later revealed.
Spoke from a wheelchair at the Democratic National Convention.
Convention keynote address from a wheelchair.

claims.statement: Barbara Jordan was born on February 21, 1936, in Houston, Texas, the youngest of three daughters, and grew up in Houston's Fifth Ward. She graduated magna cum laude from Texas Southern University in 1956 and earned a law degree from Boston University in 1959.

In 1966 she was elected to the Texas Senate, the first Black state senator since 1883. In 1972 she was elected to the U.S. House of Representatives from Houston, the first Black woman from a Southern state to serve in Congress. As a member of the House Judiciary Committee during the 1974 impeachment hearings she said, "My faith in the Constitution is whole, it is complete, it is total."
In 1976 she gave the keynote address at the Democratic National Convention, the first woman and the first African American to do so.
claims.clinical_interpretation: Anchors her public speaking in the modern social history.

claims.statement: She did not seek a fourth term and left the House in 1979, downplaying reports about her poor health and citing her "internal compass." She became the Lyndon Baines Johnson Public Service Professor at the LBJ School of Public Affairs of the University of Texas at Austin, where she taught until the early 1990s.
claims.clinical_interpretation: Anchors the modern episode in her work as a professor and public speaker in Austin, and the reports of poor health at the time she left Congress.

source_links.locator: widespread reports that failing health was the cause

claims.statement: In her later years in the House she walked with a cane, which she attributed at the time to "a bum knee"; a disability-press account written after her death says this was the first adaptive equipment her multiple sclerosis required, and that she did not openly acknowledge the disease for years.
claims.clinical_interpretation: The anchor for the modern episode, which begins about a year after she left the House, with a spastic gait and a cane. The account is a single posthumous article that reports her own public explanation at the time; it is graded probable.

claims.statement: It was later revealed that she had been diagnosed with multiple sclerosis around the time she left Congress. The year of the diagnosis is not stated in the obituaries and reference works consulted.
claims.clinical_interpretation: Anchors the modern problem of multiple sclerosis diagnosed elsewhere before the index visit. Its timing is uncertain (see CLM-0008).

source_links.locator: later, it was announced that she had the disease

claims.statement: She spoke from a wheelchair at the Democratic National Convention in 1988, and in 1992 she gave a second convention keynote address from a wheelchair, amid a lengthy battle with multiple sclerosis.
claims.clinical_interpretation: History after the modern episode; used only as context for the mobility planning.

source_links.locator: confined to a wheelchair by a degenerative disease

claims.statement: Accounts differ on when her multiple sclerosis became public. A broadcaster's profile says it was announced after she left Congress; a disability-press article says her doctors made it public only after she nearly drowned in her pool during physical therapy, which it dates to 1994 (the Texas State Historical Association dates the near-drowning to 1988 and does not link it to the disease); a reference work says her obituaries explained much she had kept private, confirming the multiple sclerosis. Her obituaries reported that she had battled multiple sclerosis for several years and moved about in a wheelchair or with a walker.
claims.clinical_interpretation: Recorded as history; the modern episode does not depend on the date of disclosure, but respects her privacy about her health.

claims.statement: She received the Presidential Medal of Freedom in 1994.
She died in Austin on January 17, 1996, at 59, of pneumonia as a complication of leukemia, and is buried in the Texas State Cemetery.
claims.clinical_interpretation: History only, long after the modern episode; not used in it.

synthetic_episode.teaching_objective: Primary care, coordinated with a multiple sclerosis neurologist, for a 44-year-old professor and public speaker who walks with a cane and has multiple sclerosis diagnosed elsewhere: confirming and classifying the disease with MRI of the brain and spine under the 2017 McDonald criteria and the 2021 MAGNIMS-CMSC-NAIMS consensus, choosing a disease-modifying therapy by course and risk under the AAN 2018 guideline, the screening and vaccination it needs before the first dose (hepatitis B serology, immunoglobulins, liver tests, blood counts, varicella and measles immunity, tuberculosis, inactivated vaccines at least two weeks ahead), its monitoring afterwards, a re-baseline MRI, recognizing relapse and pseudo-relapse, symptom care for spasticity, bladder, fatigue and heat sensitivity, mobility equipment and fall prevention, a workplace accommodation that discloses only what she chooses, bone health, mood screening, and preventive care, respecting her wish to keep her diagnosis private.

visit_schedule.purpose: Establishing primary care for multiple sclerosis diagnosed elsewhere: walking, spasticity, bladder, fatigue and heat sensitivity, work, bone health, mood, and the work-up and screening before any disease-modifying therapy
Two-week review with MRI of the brain and spine and the neurology (multiple sclerosis) consultation; vaccines before therapy
Five-week review: second vaccine doses, baclofen titration, physical therapy and readiness for the first infusion
Four-month review, six weeks after the first ocrelizumab doses: infusion tolerance, infections, blood counts, vitamin D, heat and mood
Eight-month review before the first full ocrelizumab dose: re-baseline brain MRI, blood counts and immunoglobulins, seasonal vaccines, mobility and work

hpi.narrative: Ms. Jordan returns two weeks after her first visit, after MRI of the brain and spine this morning, and is seen by Dr. Watanabe of multiple sclerosis neurology on the same day. Her walking is unchanged: she uses her cane on campus and rests after about 100 meters. She has had no new symptoms and no symptom that came on over days. Her legs are stiff in the mornings. She still gets up twice a night to pass urine and sometimes has to hurry. She has started vitamin D3. The records of her original evaluation have not arrived. She asked about treatments that might slow the disease and how often she would need to be away from work for them.

assessment_plan.assessment: MRI brain: fourteen T2 lesions, periventricular, juxtacortical and infratentorial (pons and left middle cerebellar peduncle), one enhancing right periventricular lesion. MRI spine: three cord lesions at C3, C5 and T6, each less than two segments long, with no compression. With more than a year of gradually worsening walking and no relapses, these meet the 2017 McDonald criteria for primary progressive multiple sclerosis (brain lesions in characteristic regions and two or more cord lesions), and the enhancing lesion makes it active. She is preparing for the autumn term and several speaking engagements, and her university has put the accommodations she asked for in place. She had her bone density scan this morning.

referral.question: Multiple sclerosis diagnosed elsewhere in a 44-year-old professor and public speaker who walks with a cane, with records of the original evaluation not available. Please confirm and classify the disease on the MRI booked for the morning of your visit, and advise on disease-modifying therapy, its screening and monitoring, vaccination, symptom care and MRI follow-up
referral.urgency: Within two weeks, on the same day as her two-week primary care visit
referral.pertinent_history: By her account multiple sclerosis was diagnosed elsewhere some years ago; she has no records and recalls no attack that came on over days and recovered. Her walking has worsened slowly over the past few years: she began using a cane while still in her previous public office, and now rests after about 100 meters. Leg stiffness, afternoon fatigue, heat sensitivity, urinary urgency and nocturia twice. Two near-falls and no falls in the past year. No previous disease-modifying therapy; she recalls steroid courses in the past. Today: blood pressure 124/78, weight 84.0 kg, BMI 28.1; spastic paraparetic gait with a cane; post-void residual 40 mL by bladder scan; PHQ-9 6. Results today: white cells 6.4, lymphocytes 1.9, hemoglobin 13.2 g/dL, platelets 262; creatinine 0.78 mg/dL, eGFR 96; ALT 18, AST 20, alkaline phosphatase 72 U/L, bilirubin 0.5 mg/dL; TSH 1.8; vitamin B12 520 pg/mL; 25-hydroxyvitamin D 17 ng/mL, so vitamin D3 started; IgG 1080, IgM 110, IgA 210 mg/dL; JC virus antibody index 0.14. Hepatitis B serology, varicella and measles immunity, tuberculosis blood test, HIV and hepatitis C are pending. MRI of the brain and cervical and thoracic spine with gadolinium is booked for the morning of your visit. She keeps her diagnosis private and decides who receives this letter

consultant_note.history: Ms. Jordan, a 44-year-old professor and public speaker, is seen at the request of Dr. Moss. She was told years ago that she had multiple sclerosis; the records are not available. She describes slowly worsening walking over several years, needing a cane for some time, with no attack of new symptoms over days that then recovered. She has leg stiffness, afternoon fatigue, heat sensitivity, urinary urgency and nocturia, and no visual loss or double vision. She has had steroid courses in the past and no disease-modifying therapy. She wants to know whether a treatment can slow the disease, and wants to keep teaching and speaking
consultant_note.data_reviewed: Dr. Moss's intake note and results: blood count, kidney and liver tests, TSH, vitamin B12 and immunoglobulins normal; 25-hydroxyvitamin D 17 ng/mL; JC virus antibody index 0.14, negative. Results since intake: hepatitis B surface antigen, core antibody and surface antibody negative; varicella IgG and measles, mumps and rubella IgG positive; tuberculosis blood test, HIV and hepatitis C negative. MRI this morning, brain with gadolinium: fourteen T2 lesions, periventricular, juxtacortical, and infratentorial in the pons and left middle cerebellar peduncle, with one enhancing right periventricular lesion. Cervical and thoracic spine: three cord lesions at C3, C5 and T6, each shorter than two segments, with no compression

exam.finding: Well; blood pressure 122/76
Visual acuity 20/20 in each eye; no relative afferent pupillary defect; full eye movements without nystagmus
Hip flexor strength 4 out of 5 on both sides; modified Ashworth 2 in both legs
Brisk in the legs with extensor plantar responses
Reduced vibration sense at the toes
Spastic paraparetic gait with a cane; EDSS 6.0; timed 25-foot walk 11.0 seconds

assessment.assessment: More than a year of gradually worsening disability without relapses, with T2 lesions in characteristic brain regions and two or more spinal cord lesions, meets the 2017 McDonald criteria for primary progressive multiple sclerosis without the need for spinal fluid. The enhancing lesion shows inflammatory activity, so the disease is active. B12, thyroid and HIV results and the absence of cord compression exclude the main mimics. At 44, still walking with a cane, with an enhancing lesion, she is the kind of patient most likely to benefit from therapy
Spasticity contributes to her slowness and stiffness; strength is fairly preserved, so a careful baclofen titration should not weaken her
Urgency with a low residual; safe to treat with a bladder-relaxing medicine, preferably one without anticholinergic effects on concentration

recommendations: Ocrelizumab, the therapy with evidence for primary progressive multiple sclerosis: 300 mg intravenously on day 1 and day 15, then 600 mg every 6 months, with methylprednisolone 100 mg, an antihistamine and acetaminophen beforehand and at least one hour of observation; twice-yearly infusions suit her teaching and travel

Before the first dose: she is not infected with hepatitis B but not immune, so hepatitis B vaccine; PCV20, recombinant zoster vaccine (two doses, the second after about a month), and Tdap; inactivated vaccines at least two weeks before the first dose and live vaccines at least four weeks before (none needed, as she is immune to varicella and measles); confirm no active infection on each infusion day

Monitoring: blood count with lymphocytes, liver tests and immunoglobulins before each dose; hepatitis B surface antibody after the series; prompt review of infections, persistent diarrhea or new neurological symptoms; standard breast cancer screening; no live vaccines during treatment; seasonal influenza and COVID-19 vaccines, ideally at least two weeks before an infusion
MRI: a re-baseline brain MRI three to six months after the first dose, then yearly, on the same scanner where possible and without routine gadolinium; spinal MRI only for new spinal symptoms
Spasticity: baclofen 5 mg three times a day, increasing to 10 mg three times a day once tolerated, with daily stretching and physical therapy; gabapentin is the second choice if baclofen fails
Bladder: mirabegron 25 mg daily with timed voiding and a blood pressure check at each visit
Fatigue and heat: pacing, morning teaching where she chooses, cooling garments and air conditioning, and aerobic exercise in cool water; no fatigue medicine for now

Relapse plan: new or worsening symptoms lasting more than 24 hours without fever or heat mean a same-day call; check for urinary infection first; heat or infection can bring back old symptoms for hours without new disease activity
Multiple sclerosis neurology review after the re-baseline MRI and then every six months
consultant_note.communication: Discussed with Dr. Moss, who sees her the same day. The plan was explained to Ms. Jordan, who agreed and decides who else receives this note; her reproductive plans were discussed privately and recorded in the confidential part of the chart
consultant_note.follow_up: Review after the re-baseline MRI, about seven months from now, then every six months; Dr. Moss continues primary care, vaccination and monitoring between visits
